HOUSTON — Chicago White Sox pitcher Sean Burke sat next to designated hitter Andrew Benintendi during the flight to Houston ahead of the American League wild-card series.
“Kind of just talked about playoffs, his past experiences, some stuff that we need to do,” Burke said on Tuesday afternoon at Daikin Park. “His advice was just kind of keep doing what we’ve been doing the whole year.”
That’s the approach the Sox took into the postseason. Several players are experiencing the playoffs for the first time. That includes Burke, who is in line to pitch in some role in Game 2 against the Houston Astros on Wednesday.
“I don’t think really anything needs to change,” Burke said. “We got here for a reason, and we know we have a good team, we have a talented group. I think just focusing on playing our brand of baseball is going to be good enough for us.”
Benintendi was the only White Sox player in Tuesday’s starting lineup with major-league playoff experience. He played in the postseason in 2016-18 with the Boston Red Sox. The 2018 club won the World Series.
“It’s always nice to make the playoffs,” Benintendi said on Sunday. “I haven’t played in any since 2018. I was with the Yankees, but I was hurt during their run in ’22.
“It’s exciting. It’s always fun. At the least, it’s an experience for everyone in here to dip their toes in it.”
Benintendi is one of the players shortstop Colson Montgomery leaned on.
“If you look at our lineup, it consists of a lot of kind of rookies and guys who this is our first full year,” Montgomery said before Tuesday’s game. “But also, we have a lot of veterans that have been in this scenario. (Outfielders Tommy Pham), (Benintendi), (Randal Grichuk), those guys have definitely been the people we’ve leaned on.
“And they just go out there and they’re telling us, try to make it seem like it’s another game. Go about your routines the exact same because once the game starts, it’s the same thing we’ve been playing 162 games. It can be more magnified. You can make it feel that way, but it’s just kind of the stuff they have been telling us is just take it day by day and just be you.”
Montgomery said it was important not to overanalyze the situation.
“I just feel like when you’re young and you’re hungry and you’re competitive and you’re in a scenario like this, it’s kind of like one of those things where you go out there and play,” he said. “You go out there and you compete. You don’t overanalyze a lot of things. You kind of just go out there and do what you know, and that’s play baseball. We’ve all been playing baseball for our whole lives, so in our eyes this is something that’s not anything different.
“But we’re all excited. All the young guys, we’re all pumped to be here.”
While the team did receive a special letter from Pope Leo XIV, manager Will Venable didn’t feel a special speech was necessary.
“These guys have a full understanding of what this is, even if they haven’t been here before,” Venable said on Tuesday. “We’ve talked about some of the environments and situations that we played in, especially in the second half of this year, going to Wrigley (Field to play the Cubs), going to Yankee Stadium (to play the New York Yankees), whatever it might be, and playing in those high-leverage moments and experiencing that.
“Of course, there’s nothing like the playoffs and, that’s going to be a different beast all in itself and they will have to experience that for themselves. There’s nothing that I can say that can help them feel what it’s going to feel like.”

Pete Crow-Armstrong Joins Elite Company: The 7 Players In The 40/40 Club
24-year-old Chicago Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong joined one of the rarest clubs in Major League Baseball this season. The NL MVP favorite became the seventh player in MLB history to hit 40+ home runs and steal 40+ bases in a single season.
While there are only a select few talented players who have made the club, there are several players from this generation who have made the cut and also invented clubs of their own.
Here is a list of the 7 players to make the 40/40 club:
RELATED | Top 20 All-Time Greatest Baseball Players
RELATED | MLB Players Who Played In The Little League World Series
1988 Jose Canseco – 42 HR, 40 SB, .307 AVG, .391 OBP, .569 SLG
The founding member of this club, Canseco, predicted he would achieve this milestone. He also drove in a league-leading 124 runs and posted a heavy .569 slugging percentage to coast to a unanimous AL MVP.
Canseco would lose to the Dodgers 4-1 in the World Series, winning the only game with a grand
1996 Barry Bonds – 42 HR, 40 SB, .308 AVG, .461 OBP, .615 SLG
Bonds paired pure athleticism with legendary plate discipline, combining 42 home runs and 40 stolen bases with a career-high 151 walks.
His absurd .461 OBP ensured he was constantly on base to leverage his speed, though his 9.7 WAR effort incredibly finished fifth in a hitter-dominated NL MVP vote that season.
Even with Bonds’ historic run, the Giant’s struggled this season, finishing 68-94 and 4th in the NL West.
1998 Alex Rodriguez – 42 HR, 46 SB, .310 AVG, .360 OBP, .560 SLG
At just 22 years old, A-Rod accomplished what remains the most physically demanding 40/40 season by doing it as a everyday shortstop.
He recorded an MLB-leading 213 hits, which helped him finish the season with a 43.9 Power/Speed number—the highest mark ever achieved in baseball history.
Rodriguez’s Mariners failed to reach the playoffs as well, ending the season at 76-85 and 3rd in the AL West.
2006 Alfonso Soriano – 46 HR, 41 SB, .277 AVG, .351 OBP, .560 SLG
After coming just one home run short with the Yankees in 2002, Soriano left no doubt during his single, explosive season in Washington.
He blasted 46 home runs and swiped 41 bags. Soriano’s season stands out unique because he also hit 41 doubles, creating the game’s only 40/40/40 performance.
The Nationals also failed to reach the postseason, finishing 71-91 and 5th in the NL East.
2023 Ronald Acuna Jr. – 41 HR, 73 SB, .337 AVG, .416 OBP, .596 SLG
Acuña weaponized MLB’s larger bases and rules limiting pitcher disengagements to turn the 40/40 club completely on its head.
While maintaining a career-best .337 batting average, he bashed 41 home runs and ran wild for 73 stolen bases, easily taking home NL MVP honors.
After Acuna’s record-breaking season, the superstar struggled in the postseason, hitting 2-14 and only scoring two runs. The Braves would fall in the NLDS to the Philadelphia Phillies.
2024 Shohei Ohtani – 54 HR, 59 SB, .310 AVG, .390 OBP, .646 SLG
Serving strictly as a designated hitter while rehabbing his throwing arm, Ohtani reached 40/40 in a blistering 126 games—shattering Soriano’s previous speed record of 147 games. He hit a walk-off grand slam to secure the milestone, eventually pushing his totals to 54 home runs and 59 steals to create the 50/50 club.
Ohtani is the only player so far to cap off his historic season winning the World Series, beating the Yankees in 5 games.
2026 Pete Crow-Armstrong – 45 HR, 41 SB, .280 AVG, .372 OBP, .570 SLG
Originally known as a spectacular, defense-first center fielder, PCA shocked the baseball world by developing top-tier power to accompany his elite speed. He tied for the MLB lead with 45 home runs and secured his 40th stolen base during the Cubs’ playoff-clinching victory in late September.
The Chicago Cubs will play in the Wild Card round on Tuesday.

NEW YORK – One year later, they’re right back at it. The Yankees are preparing to host the Red Sox for another American League Wild Card Series, renewing baseball’s most enduring rivalry in a best-of-three showdown.
Tuesday’s Game 1 delivers a rematch of the pairing that took place in the Bronx last October, when Cam Schlittler struck out 12 over eight scoreless innings to quiet the online chirpers and end Boston’s season, propelling his Yankees into the AL Division Series.
This time, the prize is a trip to Tropicana Field, where the Rays will be waiting to face the winner. These Yankees would gladly sign up for that.
“It's special,” Schlittler said on Monday. “Being able to get that experience last year in Game 3, it's a good feeling to go out there and get the first one.”
You don’t need to flip back to Bucky Dent to find the latest great comeback. These Red Sox seemed to have one foot on the golf course in late June, a managerial change already having taken place as they faced a 15 1/2-game deficit in the division on June 19. They rescued their season, beginning with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park from June 25-28.
“I’ve been watching Red Sox-Yankees since I was a kid. It’s Red Sox-Yankees,” said Tracy. “It’s no secret as far as the rivalry that has existed over the years for a very long time. That’s obvious to everybody. I know there’s always a little extra when those two teams meet. Beyond that, I’m not putting much more into that other than just preparing and getting ready for that series.”
How can I tune in?
Game 1 of the Red Sox-Yankees Wild Card Series is underway at Yankee Stadium. The game will be broadcast on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Tolle has become a fireballing fan favorite in Boston, just as likely to strike someone out on a 98 mph heater as he is to wrap someone into a bear hug. The Red Sox have no reservations about putting the 23-year-old into the hostile territory Yankee Stadium figures to be.
Gray, at 36, is having one of the best seasons of his career in his first year with Boston. He easily leads the Red Sox in quality starts with 20. The Yankees are one of his former teams, and the only one he didn’t perform well for in his career.
Starting pitching is the Yanks’ greatest strength going into this postseason. Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) built upon his 2025 playoff breakout to establish his place among the league’s most dominant young arms. The Walpole, Mass., product relishes taking on the Sox, for whom he once cheered, and will likely use whatever vitriol he can find on social media as potential rage fuel.
Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA) will follow in Game 2, with Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA) in line for Game 3. Fried has faced Boston twice this year, including eight scoreless innings on April 22 at Fenway Park. He last pitched Sept. 22 vs. the Rays, allowing four runs in 6 2/3 innings. Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA) is likely to be available out of the bullpen as he prepares for a potential ALDS Game 1.
What are the starting lineups?
Red Sox: Schlittler has been a big-time nemesis for the Red Sox, dating back to his coming-out party in the playoffs last year. But Boston did get a jolt from Caleb Durbin in the form of a go-ahead homer over the Green Monster against the Yankees’ ace on June 25, the win that started the 32-5 run by the Red Sox. Recently, Boston hitters have worked overtime on the Trajekt pitching machine, which can mimic any Major League starting pitcher. The Sox have struggled offensively for much of September, particularly with runners in scoring position. But they’ve also lacked multiple key lineup pieces at various parts of the month.
Yankees: Manager Aaron Boone said the Yankees view Tolle as “closer to neutral” in terms of splits, but they also tried to load their lineup with right-handed bats when they faced him in June. They did that again in Game 1, with Anthony Volpe getting the start over Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second base and Amed Rosario inserted at third base.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Red Sox: Aroldis Chapman, a former Yankee, continues to be one of the elite closers in the game at 38 years old. He has one of the league’s best setup men in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. In a significant development, the Sox placed their other key high-leverage reliever -- righty Tyron Guerrero, who frequents triple digits with his fastball -- back on the 15-day IL with a right shoulder and lat strain on Sunday’s final day of the regular season. Brayan Bello is the Swiss Army knife of the bullpen, available for bulk relief and also taking down a couple of innings when necessary. The most intriguing roster question for the Red Sox heading into the series was answered Tuesday morning, when Garrett Crochet, who started the season as the ace but hasn’t pitched since April 25, was activated for this series.
Yankees: David Bednar finished his first full season in the Bronx with 35 saves and a 2.50 ERA in 63 appearances, the closer ahead of a relief crew that leaned heavily upon Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick and Tim Hill in the late innings. The Yankees didn’t make a bullpen acquisition at the Trade Deadline, but they added pieces down the stretch by picking up Michael Fulmer and John Schreiber, both of whom could be called upon for valuable outs. Will Warren is also converting into a relief role and could provide length. Ryan Weathers appears to be in play as a potential bullpen piece, adding a big arm to the mix.
Any injuries of note?
Red Sox: Contreras got smoked on the knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie on Sept. 17, but took two at-bats in the final game of the regular season on Sunday and should be good to go. Guerrero is a big loss in the bullpen for this series. Justin Slaten, a key leverage reliever for Boston the past three seasons, is also out with a right flexor injury.
Masataka Yoshida, one of the few Boston hitters who performed against the Yankees in last year’s postseason series, won’t factor in this year. He’s been out since Aug. 16 with a hamstring strain and likely won’t make it back this season.
Yankees: No story has occupied more space recently than Aaron Judge’s right soleus strain, which typically requires weeks on the injured list. Judge tried to convince the Yankees' brass that he could give it a go for the Wild Card round, but sources confirmed to MLB.com on Tuesday that Judge would would not be on the Wild Card roster vs. Boston. Meanwhile, Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham have both been hitting and running. Weathers is out with a flexor strain but hopes to return.
Who is hot and who is not?
Red Sox: Anthony has understandably had some ups and downs after missing nearly four months with a right hand/wrist injury, but he slashed .333/.375/.633 in his final eight games of the season. From a pitching standpoint, Bello has been a force since he returned from the Minors, posting a 2.11 ERA in 14 appearances, including three starts.
Rutschman has had a hard time getting his bat going since joining the Red Sox at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline but had a two-hit game in Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader against the Cubs. Abreu is notoriously streaky and he’s been mostly cold in September (.207/.286/.329, one homer, six RBIs). If past history is any indication, he could heat up again in a hurry.
Yankees: Rice hit his team-leading 40th and 41st home runs on Sept. 23 vs. Tampa Bay, claiming a share of the AL lead until Pete Alonso passed him on Friday. Rice, a Cohasset, Mass., product, has belted six homers in September. Bellinger has been productive all month, tying Jones (14) for second on the team in RBIs behind Lombard (16). García enjoyed a productive stretch after arriving in a midseason trade but recently endured a long hitless streak. Ryan McMahon has struggled to produce all year.
Anything else fans might want to know?
This marks the seventh time the rivalry has gone to the postseason stage – all since 1999. Fittingly, the teams have split the first six matchups.
The Yankees had the series edge over Boston this season, winning seven of 13 contests. The Yanks swept three games at Fenway in April and split a pair in June, then were swept in a four-game series in Boston later that month. New York took three of four from the Sox in late August, their most recent meeting.
Though Anthony was a big part of the ‘25 Red Sox team, he missed the postseason with a left oblique strain. He is Boston’s leadoff hitter and could have a big impact on this series. During the World Baseball Classic for Team USA, Anthony displayed the ability to perform on a big stage.

The Astros, who roared back from an early-season deficit to win their eighth American League West title in 10 seasons Sunday, return to the playoffs following a one-year absence to face the upstart White Sox, who led the AL Central for much of the season before settling for the final Wild Spot in the AL.
While this series might not attract the attention of the AL’s other Wild Card Series -- the Yankees and Red Sox -- Astros-White Sox is an intriguing battle featuring a playoff-tested Houston team that has star power in AL Most Valuable Player favorite Yordan Alvarez, former World Series MVP Jeremy Peña and Jose Altuve, one of this generation’s greatest postseason performers, against a Chicago team with some up-and-coming stars.
“I feel like we did the hardest part, which was to get in,” Alvarez said.
The White Sox are led by Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, one of the best power-hitting duos in baseball. Murakami slammed 35 home runs as a rookie, and Vargas had 33 homers and should receive some downballot MVP votes.
"It feels good,” White Sox designated hitter Andrew Benintendi said. “I think that kind of hit a certain point of the year where you slot yourself in there. Now it’s officially over. The real season starts now."
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 1 of the White Sox-Astros Wild Card Series is underway at Daikin Park. The game is being broadcast on Peacock and NBCSN.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
White Sox: Hagen Smith, LHP
Key Stats: 1.29 ERA, 28 IP, 13.1 K/9
With a chance to win the American League Central, the White Sox used Sean Burke (11-7, 3.34), Davis Martin (9-8, 3.95) and Anthony Kay (10-9, 4.44) against the last-place Rockies this weekend. Burke is likely lined up for Game 2 behind Game 1 starter Hagen Smith, who got the nod in an expected "bullpen-type game" from manager Will Venable on Monday. Smith is a largely untested rookie, but during his 18 games and 28 innings, he has induced some ugly-looking swings from the opposition.
Astros: AJ Blubaugh, RHP
Key Stats: Led MLB relievers with 96 IP
The 25-year-old rookie will start Tuesday’s Game 1 as the opener of what will be a bullpen game. Blubaugh threw 15 pitches in relief on Friday against the A’s, allowing one run in two-thirds of an inning.
Blubaugh led the Major Leagues with 27 relief appearances of at least two innings this season, the most by an Astros pitcher since Dave Veres had 27 in 1995. Blubaugh led all relievers with a career-high 96 innings. He has thrown more than two innings in only five games this season.
Blubaugh faced the White Sox three times in the regular season, allowing no runs, four hits and two walks while striking out three in four innings.
What are the starting lineups?
White Sox: With the Astros going with a bullpen game, the White Sox are trotting out this lineup.
Astros: The last three spots in the order are occupied by outfielders. Rookie Lucas Spence, who hit four homers in the season’s final series, earned the start in center, and Cam Smith will be in right field, hitting eighth.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
White Sox: Venable is not set on one lockdown closer, although Grant Taylor is coming off a dominant campaign with a 2.25 ERA and 106 strikeouts in 84 innings. So, Taylor could be used for two innings in the sixth and seventh, or try to finish off a victory in the ninth. The same holds true for relievers such as Sean Newcomb, Bryan Hudson and the rookie additions of Smith and Noah Schultz.
Astros: A seven-inning outing by starter Hayden Wesneski on Saturday and Sunday’s blowout win in the regular-season finale have Houston’s bullpen in really good shape heading into the postseason, especially with the Astros contemplating a bullpen game for Tuesday. They could get multiple innings out of the bullpen from Josh Hendrickson, Miguel Ullola and AJ Blubaugh in an effort to get the ball to setup man Bryan Abreu and closer Josh Hader, who finished the season with a 1.01 ERA and 26-for-26 in save chances. He hasn’t pitched since Wednesday.
Any injuries of note?
White Sox: Chase Meidroth has been dealing with left hamstring discomfort, among myriad nagging injuries. He sat out most of the weekend against the Rockies after leaving early from Thursday’s playoff-clincher in Kansas City, but should be available Tuesday.
Astros: Isaac Paredes fouled a ball off his knee Saturday in West Sacramento and was in the lineup for Sunday’s season finale, but the Astros were so concerned about the knee that they called up infielder Raynel Delgado to give them some coverage at third base. Center fielders Daulton Varsho (wrist) and Brice Matthews (knee) both landed on the IL last week, so neither will be available for the Wild Card Series.
Who is hot and who is not?
White Sox: Colson Montgomery was a deserving All-Star candidate who was passed over, but has found rough going since the break. In fact, Montgomery finished the season with a .197 average and set the single-season Major League record with 227 strikeouts. He spoke eloquently pregame Sunday about being focused on doing anything to help the team and looking for a reset starting with the playoffs.
Miguel Vargas’ season has been a revelation overall, with 33 homers, 31 doubles, 22 stolen bases, 101 walks, 93 RBIs and 106 runs scored. Munetaka Murakami also seems back on track, with his 35 homers tying Ron Kittle for the second-highest single-season home run total for a White Sox rookie trailing only Jose Abreu (36 in 2014).
Astros: Yordan Alvarez won the AL batting title and will likely add his first AL Most Valuable Player to his resume following a season in which he slashed .316/.432/.601 with 105 runs, 34 doubles, 42 homers, 106 RBIs and 109 walks. Jeremy Peña slashed .353/.358/.706 with five homers and nine RBIs in the Astros’ final 12 games.
Christian Walker had a 1.167 OPS with four homers in the last eight games, Yainer Diaz slashed .350/.377/.581 with six homers and 17 RBIs in 34 games since Aug. 16 and rookie Lucas Spence was 6-for-15 with four homers, a triple and nine RBIs in the final four games of the season.
Taylor Trammell finished the season 0-for-20.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Astros have lost seven consecutive home playoff games, dating to 2023.
• This is the third time the Astros and White Sox have met in the playoffs. The White Sox swept Houston in the 2005 World Series, and the Astros eliminated the White Sox in four games in the 2021 ALDS.

The Boston Red Sox will be taking on the New York Yankees in the American League wild-card round this year, which is a rematch from last season.
Boston was able to clinch a spot in the postseason following an impressive run during the middle of the year to get back into the race. But the Red Sox couldn’t do enough to overtake the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East, and now they will be entering a three-game series that will determine their fate.
The longtime rivals are gearing up for Game 1 of the highly anticipated series, with each trying to make a statement against the other. New York won the season series 7-6, but the entire matchup was extremely close, leading to the thought that this playoff matchup will be as well.
Last season, the Yankees defeated the Red Sox in three games to move on to the ALDS. Boston will be looking for some revenge here, and the series is again being played in New York.
Jarren Duran Decision Made by Red Sox
Ahead of Game 1, the Red Sox have now released the lineup that they will use against the Yankees. Within the lineup, outfielder Jarren Duran will be hitting seventh for Boston today.
Duran will be playing in left field.
Red Sox 9/29
R. Anthony DH
A. Rutschman C
W. Contreras 1B
W. Abreu RF
C. Rafaela CF
N. Sogard 2B
J. Duran LF
T. Story SS
C. Durbin 3B
P. Tolle SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 29, 2026
Duran has seen a tough season at the plate take place, and it’s hurt the overall ceiling of this Red Sox team. Overall, the former All-Star has hit .207 with 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, and 21 stolen bases, while posting an OPS of .627.
Boston has been waiting for Duran to break out of his slump all season long, but to this point, nothing has worked. But if he can get his bat going in the playoffs, his struggles from the regular season will be forgiven.
Can Red Sox Take Down Yankees?
For the Red Sox to win this series, guys like Duran are going to need to step up heavily. New York will be without star Aaron Judge due to injury, and the Red Sox need to take advantage of this fact.
Boston’s pitching staff will be counted on heavily in this series as they try to match the strong starting rotation from the Yankees. But luckily for the Red Sox, the team will be getting back ace left-hander Garrett Crochet from injury.
It has been a long time coming for Crochet, with him last pitching on April 25 for this team. Crochet has been trying to come back all year, but the Red Sox finally saw progress over the last few weeks, and he has been added to the playoff roster.
If Crochet can make an impact as a relief pitcher, it could go a long way for this team against the Yankees. Boston is behind the eight ball when it comes to the pitching in the series, and Crochet gives them at least a fighting chance.
The Red Sox and Yankees will kick off the opening game of the series at 5:00 p.m. PT/8:00 p.m. ET from Yankee Stadium.

Apple vs. Microsoft. Coke vs. Pepsi. Marvel vs. DC. Ford vs. General Motors.
All child’s play compared to Yankees vs. Red Sox.
Though seeded as Wild Cards, New York and Boston are heavyweight entries in the 2026 postseason field. And only one can advance out of the best-of-three Wild Card Series that begins -- and takes place entirely -- in the Bronx on Tuesday.
The Yankees have survived most of the season without captain Aaron Judge, while the Red Sox survived a brutal start that had them 14 games under .500 in late June.
But who will survive this short and scintillating series at Yankee Stadium? Let’s break it down, position by position, and we are sure to find the unmistakably correct prediction, right? Right?!
Catcher
Austin Wells just hasn’t produced with the consistency he did in his Rookie of the Year finalist season in 2024 or the power he had in last year’s 20-homer, 20-double campaign. He’s a fantastic framer and blocker, and that could matter more in the postseason than his bat given the pitching staff’s increased importance in a short series. But Rutschman has those same strengths, along with an elite caught stealing track record, to go with higher offensive upside in a season in which he’s posted an above-average OPS+.
Edge: Red Sox
First base
The Red Sox have a major asset, but also a major question mark in Willson Contreras. He was a monumental offseason pickup in a trade with the Cardinals. The veteran produced his best offensive season yet, with an OPS over .900 and career-highs in homers and RBIs.
But when Contreras was plunked in the hand by a pitch late in the regular season, it complicated the equation. As of this writing, it was still not clear if he would suit up for the Wild Card Series. Even if he does, he might need some time to get back in the swing of things, given the impact hand discomfort can have on a power stroke.
So the Yankees’ successful midseason acquisition of Luis García Jr. looms large here. After an offensive breakthrough with the Nationals, he’s remained an above-average producer in pinstripes, finishing off his 30-homer season. And the Yanks have a dangerous platoon option in Paul Goldschmidt, the consummate pro who still does big damage to lefties – no small tool in their chest given the lefty leaning complexion of the Red Sox’s starting staff.
Edge: Yankees
Second base
Between the trade of the disappointing Marcelo Mayer and a late-season injury to Anthony Siegler, the Red Sox are left piecing things together here with Nick Sogard and veteran Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Sogard’s contact skills can play up in the postseason even if he doesn’t produce much power.
But the Yankees have higher upside here. Though Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s walk year saw statistical regression, he ultimately provided league-average offense with north of 40 steals. He could augment his open-market asking price with a strong showing.
Edge: Yankees
Shortstop
Trevor Story was sidelined for the Sox for about three months with a sports hernia that required surgery. He showed signs of offensive life in September, but this will nevertheless go down as one of his worst seasons at the plate in limited time.
The Yankees look like they have a star in the making in George Lombard Jr. While no one knows how the fresh-faced 21-year-old, who only debuted on Aug. 4, will perform under the bright lights of the postseason, he’s already had some huge hits for the Yanks and his plate discipline, high baseball IQ, fluid actions and plus speed all make him dangerous in a short series.
Edge: Yankees
Third base
The hot corner has been cold to the Yankees this year. Veteran Ryan McMahon’s first full season in the Bronx has been a drastic disappointment and his right-handed-hitting complement Amed Rosario hasn’t been much better. The Yankees were toying with the idea of working former shortstop Anthony Volpe here.
As for Boston, while replacing free-agent departure Alex Bregman was a tall order, a trade for Caleb Durbin, a reigning NL Rookie of the Year finalist with the Brewers, has paid enormous dividends. Durbin looked lost in the headlights for his first couple months in a major market, but his midseason ignition matched that of the club at large. He has great range at third, is among the more difficult batters in MLB to strike out and logged 25 doubles for the second straight season.
Edge: Red Sox
Left field
After getting spurned by Juan Soto in free agency the previous winter, the Yankees did not let Cody Bellinger get away. In his second season with the Yanks, the former NL MVP became an All-Star Game MVP in the midst of providing his usual disciplined, contact-and-power profile at the plate and elite defense in the grass. He’s been on this postseason stage plenty of times before.
There was hope in Boston that Roman Anthony would break out into superstardom this season. But a significant finger ligament injury early in the season got in the way, opening the door for Jarren Duran to see the bulk of time in left while producing an OPS+ more than 20% below league average. Anthony returned in late August, and it should shock no one if this postseason turns into his coming-out party. But for now, we’ve got to go with the more accomplished veteran here.
Edge: Yankees
Center field
The Sox had another late-season health scare with Ceddanne Rafaela, their rangy, speedy power-armed gem in center field. Rafaela was finishing up his finest offensive season to date when he suffered a right quad strain a few weeks back. But a clean MRI in the season’s final week allowed him to return.
Meanwhile, Trent Grisham’s September hamstring strain gave the Yankees their own center-field concern. Grisham’s absence allowed 25-year-old rookie Spencer Jones to showcase his excellent raw power and athleticism. Grisham could be back for this series. But Rafaela’s offensive breakthrough and Gold Glove defense carry the way here.
Edge: Red Sox
Right field
Judge’s calf injury is probably the biggest X-factor in the entire postseason field. The Yankees were cagey about its severity, and manager Aaron Boone said the club was preparing for a Wild Card Series without the captain. Judge was intent on trying to make his way back. But ultimately, Judge was left off the Bombers' Wild Card roster, so they'll be down one of the best hitters on the planet.
For the Red Sox, Wilyer Abreu is ready for his close-up. He was a durable doubles machine who also reached career highs in homers and RBIs, he dramatically improved his production against left-handed pitching, and he has range and a mammoth arm in right. His surge was essential in the Sox returning to the postseason.
Edge: Red Sox
Designated hitter
With Masataka Yoshida out with a hamstring strain, Boston will utilize a DH platoon that includes Roman Anthony against righties and Jahmai Jones against lefties.
In a season that has included so little Judge, the Yankees have gotten a ton out of Ben Rice. Last season’s surprise ascendence for the New England native has proven to be only an appetizer. Rice showed he can mash both lefties and righties alike in clearing the 40-homer threshold, getting selected as a first-time All-Star and earning down-ballot MVP support.
Edge: Yankees
Starting pitching
Cam Schlittler’s likely Cy Young-winning breakthrough in 2026 came on the heels of him carving up the Red Sox club he grew up rooting for in last year’s Wild Card Series. He pairs with Max Fried and Gerrit Cole to give the Yankees a terrifying top end of the rotation in this short series, even if the finish on Cole’s pitches is not yet what it was prior to Tommy John.
While the Yankees deserve the edge here, that’s not to suggest the Sox are slouches in the starting department. That they got to this point essentially without Garrett Crochet took a lot of fortitude, and Payton Tolle’s fantastic rookie campaign was one of the most fun storylines of the season. Sonny Gray remains an absolute command artist in his age-36 season, and Ranger Suarez was a terrific offseason signing who drastically limits the kind of hard contact that can change games in October.
Still, it’s the Yanks here.
Edge: Yankees
Bullpen
These are two top-five relief units in terms of both ERA and expected ERA. Both are excellent at suppressing long balls, which is crucial in October.
The Yankees have a strong ninth-inning anchor in David Bednar, whose elite ability to generate chase with his four-steam/split/curve mix can neutralize even the biggest bats. Paul Blackburn has gone from oft-injured starter to absolute force of nature in the setup role, and Brent Headrick has also undergone a massive transformation as a member of the Yankees ‘pen, for whom he has emerged as a whiff machine. The strength of the starting staff has trickled down to a Yankees bullpen that ranks among the lowest innings workloads of any relief unit in MLB this season.
With Tyron Guerrero’s recent return from injury and the presence of Garrett Whitlock, Greg Weissert and lefty Jovani Morán, the Sox are well-situated in their bridge to the ninth. And in the ninth, they’ve got the ageless Aroldis Chapman, whose age-38 season has seen him produce yet another sub-2.00 ERA, another ERA+ more than 100% better than league average and upper-echelon velo and strikeout rates. He recently returned from a late-season lat issue. Between Chapman’s presence and the possibility that Crochet’s elite arsenal impacts the ‘pen in his potential return from injury, the Red Sox earn the edge.
Edge: Red Sox
Prediction
The Yankees were the better team in record and run differential, and they did it mostly without Judge. They hold the home-field and rotation advantages, have a higher run-scoring baseline and are, therefore, the clear favorites.
All reasons why I’m taking the Red Sox in three. Because baseball.

By Evan Woodbery, mlive.com
DETROIT — Scott Harris didn’t have to spend much time searching for the stretch that doomed the Detroit Tigers’ season.
That miserable May is right there for everyone to see.
The Tigers went 6-22, tumbled into last place in the American League Central and spent the rest of the summer trying to recover. They never really did, finishing 76-86 and missing the postseason for the first time in three years.
Less than 24 hours after the season ended, Harris offered his explanation for how a team that entered the year with championship aspirations wound up 10 games under .500.
“This season, and the fact that we’re sitting here right now, is a missed opportunity for this organization, plain and simple,” the Tigers’ president of baseball operations said Monday at Comerica Park. “We’ve got to get better.”
Some of those explanations are easier to quantify than others. Here’s Harris’ assessment of what went wrong.
The May meltdown
There are a lot of ways to dissect a 162-game season, but the brutal 28-game stretch early in the season was a gut punch to the Tigers’ plans to contend in 2026.
“There are a lot of reasons why we’re sitting here and not in the playoffs right now,” Harris said. “One of them really sticks out above the rest for me. You can’t go 6-22 in a month and expect to punch your ticket to the postseason at this level.”
“I think one of the things that I’m really struggling to process about this year is, in many ways, this roster performed quite well for five months, excluding May.”
Before and after May, the Tigers went 70-64. Even more notably, Harris said, they ranked second in baseball in team ERA, second in wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) and posted a plus-119 run differential.
“That’s playoff-worthy. If anything, our record probably should have been even better than 70-64, given the underlying run production and run prevention.”
Why did May happen?
Harris’ answer began with injuries.
Injuries, and a roster that couldn’t absorb them
The Tigers were hit unusually hard by injuries.
Second baseman Gleyber Torres, outfielder Kerry Carpenter, reliever Will Vest and, of course, ace starter Tarik Skubal missed most or all of the month.
Even without Skubal and Vest, run prevention generally wasn’t the biggest problem. The lineup cratered, with significant at-bats going to fill-ins like Gage Workman and Zack Short. Role players like Jahmai Jones, Zach McKinstry and Matt Vierling were pressed into larger roles while mired in prolonged slumps.
“Our roster never really saw the light of day,” Harris said. “We built a roster that we thought was talented, that many people in this room thought was really talented, and they never all actually got on the field at the same time.”
“It’s really hard to have an honest conversation about this organization in the 2026 season without noting that we put 41 players on the injured list on our 40-man roster this year,” Harris said.
“It’s not an excuse. But at some point, you get to a volume of injuries that becomes destabilizing to your ability to manage a roster. I think it did. It really hurt us in certain sections of this year.”
But Harris also said he didn’t build enough depth beyond the active roster to handle what happened.
“Upon reflection, our inability to overcome adversity in real time starts with me,” Harris said. “I didn’t build enough depth into this roster this year. The vulnerabilities in this roster got exposed in May, and it cost us.”
Harris said Detroit entered the season knowing it would become deeper as the summer progressed, with prospects like center fielder Max Clark slated to arrive later.
“I think the main mistake that I made was our depth was coming a little bit too late, basically in all facets of our roster,” Harris said.
The Tigers were also reluctant to add players who might eventually block those prospects. That left them trying short-term fixes like Short and, later, outfielder James Outman.
“We didn’t want to block young players,” Harris said. “We didn’t want to trade for depth players that were ultimately going to box Max out of the big leagues. So we were trying to thread that needle, and I think it probably was a mistake in the end.
“We probably should have just strengthened our depth and made sure that we could get through April and May intact.”
Harris said Detroit was particularly thin with up-the-middle defenders, back-end relievers and starting-pitching depth.
“We couldn’t really afford to lose back-end relievers,” he said. “We couldn’t really afford to lose starting depth. And we couldn’t really afford to have our pinch hitters’ performance sag in leverage spots.”
All that happened in May.
“Could we afford to have all (of that) happen at the same time? No, clearly not,” Harris said. “We went 6-22 that month, and so I feel very responsible for that.”
Too much mixing and matching
The Tigers have built much of their identity by playing the matchups, mixing and matching and asking players to be versatile.
But Harris suggested for the first time that they may have become too reliant on it.
When role players do well, like Andy Ibáñez in 2024 and Jahmai Jones in 2025, it’s a huge boost in high-leverage moments.
But when players in those roles struggle, as they did during key points in 2026, it can be devastating.
Harris sees the arrival of more players like Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark, who the Tigers believe can contribute both offensively and defensively and play nine innings every day, as a way to reduce that dependence.
“I think we’re probably going to start playing differently a little bit,” Harris said. “We’re going to be less reliant on pinch-hit appearances. We’re going to be less reliant on the mixing and matching because we have more two-way players growing through the system that can help us both defensively and offensively.”
Lagging in leverage
Based on their run differential, the Tigers had an expected record of 89-73, not 76-86.
Of course, baseball doesn’t work that way. But the gap between what actually happened and what their run differential suggests should have happened is one of the most perplexing storylines of 2026.
“When you take a look at our season, our run differential says one thing and our record says something very different,” Harris said.
“If we had played up to our run differential, we probably would have won the division again.”
“That doesn’t matter,” he added. “I can’t stand up here and just cite different metrics and tell you this is what we should have done and act like we did it. We didn’t do it.”
“So the question that I’m going to ask myself is: How do we play in a way that either meets or exceeds our run production and run prevention performance, our underlying performance?”
It’s no secret the Tigers won a lot of blowouts and lost a ton of close games. They went an astonishing 23-52 in games decided by two runs or fewer.
That’s largely because the Tigers performed better in low- and medium-leverage situations than they did when the leverage spiked.
The numbers were particularly stark among relievers.
Tigers relievers faced 370 batters in high-leverage situations and posted a jaw-dropping 9.21 ERA (5.62 FIP). Opponents posted an .855 OPS against them and hit a league-high 19 home runs in those situations. A staggering 21.8 percent of opposing fly balls landed in the seats. No other team was even close in that category.
Maybe that’s bad luck. But it’s also bad news for any team trying to contend.
“We really struggled in high leverage,” Harris said. “We’ve got to get to the bottom of that. We’ve got to figure out why that happens.”
Harris said sometimes the problem was that the game never should have reached a high-leverage situation in the first place.
“We’ve got to do a better job of staying out of those high-leverage situations,” Harris said.
That means looking beyond the final pitch of a loss.
“There were a number of games that we saw this year where we got walked off or our bullpen blew a late lead that I don’t think you can actually put on our bullpen,” Harris said.
“Some of them you can, for sure. But some of them you can’t.
“Some of them you can actually look deeper into the game and you could find the core issue, which was we didn’t create separation before, or we made a misplay in the third inning and coughed up one or two runs, or we made a baserunning mistake in the fifth inning,” Harris said.
“We let our opponent stay in the game, create this one- and two-run game, and then we ultimately lost it.”
Harris believes the changing makeup of the roster can help with that.
The Tigers are getting younger, faster and, in Harris’ view, more athletic. He expects that to mean better defense, more aggressive baserunning and more ways to create separation without simply waiting for a home run.
“We’re going to take the extra base. We’re also going to steal bases. And we’re also going to put a lot more pressure, and that’s all going to contribute to creating separation when we’re not hitting,” Harris said.
“We’re still going to hit, but we’re also going to be able to flex different muscles at different times that can help us stay out of those high-leverage situations.”
Harris said the Tigers are already conducting what he called a “pre-mortem” on the 2027 roster, trying to anticipate next year’s vulnerabilities before they arise.
“What if this happens? What are we going to do? What if this happens? What are we going to do?” Harris said.
That includes underperformance as well as injuries.
“If a guy gets out of the gate really slow, what are we going to do?” Harris said. “Those are the questions we have to ask ourselves.
“When I talk about learning lessons from the season, that’s one of the lessons that I’ve learned.”

item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.

The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.

item.content:encoded:
New York Mets fans hoping that the team makes Tarik Skubal their top offseason priority received some bad news in a new rumor.
On Sunday, a very disappointing season for the Mets came to a close with a 6-4 loss to the Washington Nationals. The team with the second-highest payroll in MLB entered the offseason with World Series hopes and instead finished last in the National League East with a 74-88 record.
After addressing who will be their full-time manager — they signed interim skipper Andy Green to a three-year deal last week — and adding more talented minds to the front office, the club will now shift to improving the roster for 2027.
President David Stearns revealed that the starting staff will be the part of the roster the front office focuses on improving. That is why making a strong push to sign the two-time Cy Young winner would make sense. The combo of NL Rookie of the Year candidate Nolan McLean and Skubal could be a dynamite duo for many years.
However, according to The Athletic's Will Sammon, the Mets will go bargain shopping to add pitchers for a specific reason.
"League sources said the club is expected to aggressively pursue options at the lower end of the starting pitcher market for better depth. For two straight years, Stearns and his front office failed to cushion the rotation with enough viable alternatives in case of injury or poor performance. In 2025, Griffin Canning's injury was too big of a burden. In May, the Mets failed to overcome Clay Holmes' fibula injury in time to save their season. It simply can't happen again."
The strategy makes sense. And Sammon notes that good starting pitching depth has played a role in the consistent success of teams like the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. However, for fans hoping the team makes big moves to improve the rotation this summer, more discount shopping by Stearns will further frustrate them.

29 Sep 2026, 06:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Frerker)
The Chicago Cubs eliminated the San Diego Padres from the postseason a year ago and then scored 55 runs while going 5-1 against them this season.
But nobody is expecting that type of one-sided matchup to continue as the Padres are hotter than lava entering Tuesday night's National League wild-card series opener against visiting Chicago.
The Padres (91-71) are a sizzling 41-18 since July 24, transforming a bumbling campaign into a third straight postseason berth, a first in franchise history.
In the final days of the season, San Diego overtook the Cubs (89-73) to secure the No. 4 seed, granting the Padres home-field advantage in the best-of-three series. Chicago, the No. 5 seed, hosted at Wrigley Field last season and beat the Padres in three games in the wild-card round.
Playing the series at pitcher-friendly Petco Park could lessen the Cubs' offensive advantage. Chicago led the majors with 850 runs this season, while the Padres scored 722.
The Cubs feature leading NL MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong, who recorded a 40-40 season by tying for the major league lead with 45 homers and adding 41 steals. He also led the majors with 84 extra-base hits and 119 runs.
Crow-Armstrong batted .364 (8-for-22) with four homers and 10 RBIs against San Diego this season.
'I'm looking forward to playing a really good ballclub and getting another crack at them and starting this playoffs off on a high note,' Crow-Armstrong said Monday.
San Diego's Manny Machado batted a career-low .217 but smacked 30 homers, marking the eighth time in his career he has hit at least that many.
More important to the Padres is Fernando Tatis Jr., who didn't hit his first homer until May 30 and had just five at the All-Star break. He hit 20 blasts after the break and was a major catalyst for the team's torrid 59-game finish.
'It's a baseball game. We have to get 27 outs and hopefully be the last team standing,' Machado said.
Right-hander Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA) will start for the Padres against Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91).
King has made two career postseason starts, both in 2024 for the Padres. The most memorable one came in Game 1 of the wild-card series against the Atlanta Braves when he tossed seven shutout innings and struck out 12.
King gave up one hit and struck out three in one inning of relief against the Cubs in the 2025 postseason series, his lone appearance against them with the Padres. He also twice faced Chicago in relief when he was with the New York Yankees.
'Very professional lineup,' King said of the Cubs. 'They were first in runs this year and it shows. I keep saying that when the pitcher executes, we have the upper hand so I have to make sure I am executing throughout and putting up as many zeroes as I can.'
Chicago's Alex Bregman is 7-for-8 with two doubles against King.
Bregman surged over the final two months, delivering 17 homers and 46 RBIs to get his season outputs to 28 and 93, respectively.
Bregman is playing with multiple fractures in his left cheek after getting hit by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch during a game on Sept. 20.
Boyd, 35, is 0-1 with a 1.66 ERA in seven playoff appearances (six starts). He was 0-1 with a 2.79 ERA in three starts for Chicago last postseason and gave up one run and four hits over 4 1/3 innings when the Cubs beat the Padres in Game 1 of last year's wild-card series.
'The Padres are one of the hottest teams in baseball the past few weeks,' Boyd said. 'That's not surprising. We've seen them firsthand -- this year, last year. I always firmly believe that it's more about what's in this clubhouse and less about what's on the other side. Take care of your business.'
Boyd is 2-1 with a 4.43 ERA in four regular-season outings against San Diego. Machado is 9-for-20 (.450) with a homer and four doubles against Boyd.
The winner of this series faces the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Division Series.
--Field Level Media
